# **Markov Models** {background-color="#40666e" footer="false"}

## Markov Models

### What are they

A Markov model is a statistical tool used to model [systems that change over time]{.alert}
and where the [future depends only on the present]{.alert}.

::: fragment
Common examples include:

- Weather transitions
- Movement or behavioural states
- Progression of cognitive decline
  - [This is where my work is focused]{.alert}
:::

## Markov Models

### What are they

::: incremental
-   The model hinges on the [Markov property]{.alert}:
    -   Let $X_t$ denote an arbitrary state at time $t$, where
        $X_t \in S = \{1, 2, \dots, K\}$.
    -   Transition to state $j$ at $t + 1$ depends [only]{.alert} on state $i$
        at $t$.
:::

:::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Markov property

$$
P(X_{t+1} = j \; \vert \; X_t = i, X_{t-1} = i_{t-1}, \dots X_0 = i_0) = P(X_{t+1} = j \; \vert \; X_t = i)
$$

:::
::::

# **Goodness of fit** {background-color="#40666e" footer="false"}

## Goodness of fit {footer="false"}

### Residual analysis

In ordinary regression settings, residuals measure the difference between what
the model predicts and what we observe.

They are central for diagnosing:

::: incremental
-   Misfit
-   Non-linearity
-   Outliers
:::

:::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## Residuals typically rely on a clear [“predicted value”]{.alert} for each observation.
:::
::::

## Goodness of fit {footer="false"}

### Residual analysis

```{r}
#| label: fig-1
#| fig-cap: "Observed data"

set.seed(432)

# Hours of study per week (our x variable)
study_hours <- rnorm(10, mean = 7, sd = 2)

# Exam scores (our y variable)
exam_scores <- 25 + 5 * study_hours + rnorm(10, mean = 0, sd = 2)

test_data <- data.frame(study_hours = ceiling(study_hours), exam_scores = ceiling(exam_scores))

# Plotting ---------------------------------------------------------------------
fig_1 <- test_data |>
    ggplot(aes(x = study_hours, y = exam_scores)) +
    geom_point(size = 4) +
    labs(x = "Number of hours studied", y = "Exam score") +
    theme_pres()

fig_1
```

## Goodness of fit {footer="false"}

### Residual analysis

```{r}
#| label: fig-2
#| fig-cap: "Observed data with fitted model"

# Adding regression line
fig_2 <- fig_1 +
    geom_smooth(formula = y ~ x, method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = palette_okabe_ito(5))

fig_2
```

## Goodness of fit {footer="false"}

### Residual analysis

```{r}
#| label: fig-3
#| fig-cap: "Observed data, fitted model, and predicted values"

# Fitting model
fit <- glm(exam_scores ~ study_hours, data = test_data)

# Getting predicted values
predicted_vals <- test_data |>
    dplyr::mutate(preds = coef(fit)[1] + coef(fit)[2] * study_hours)

# Adding predicted values to plot
fig_3 <- fig_2 +
    geom_point(
        data = predicted_vals,
        aes(x = study_hours, y = preds),
        size = 3.5,
        colour = palette_okabe_ito(4)
        )

fig_3
```

## Goodness of fit {footer="false"}

### Residual analysis

```{r}
#| label: fig-4
#| fig-cap: "Residuals: distance between observed and fitted values"

fig_4 <- fig_3 +
    geom_segment(
        data = predicted_vals,
        aes(x = study_hours, xend = study_hours,
            y = exam_scores,  yend = preds),
        colour = ggokabeito::palette_okabe_ito(2),
        linewidth = 1.5, linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.5
        )

fig_4
```

## Goodness of fit {footer="false"}

### What about Markov Models

Markov Models dont deal with predicted values, but rather [probabilities]{.alert}.

::: fragment
$$
P = \begin{bmatrix}
P(A \rightarrow A) \quad P(A \rightarrow B) \\
P(B \rightarrow A) \quad P(B \rightarrow B)
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
0.6 \quad 0.4 \\
0.7 \quad 0.3
\end{bmatrix}
$$
:::

::: fragment
For state **A**, the model predicts a probability vector:

$$
P(X_{t+1} \; \vert \; X_t = A) = (0.6, 0.4)
$$

But in reality we observe [one transition]{.alert}:
$A \rightarrow A \quad A \rightarrow B$

A residual like $y - \hat{y}$ no longer make any mathematical sense.
:::

# **Simulation Study** {background-color="#40666e" footer=false}

## Simulation Study

### Transition matrices

```{r}

transitions <- tibble::tribble(
  ~from , ~to , ~obs , ~pred ,
  "A"   , "A" , 0.83 , 0.60  ,
  "A"   , "B" , 0.17 , 0.40  ,
  "B"   , "A" , 0.33 , 0.70  ,
  "B"   , "B" , 0.66 , 0.30
)

transitions |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(obs:pred),
    names_to = "transition",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = to, y = from, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = value),
    size = 4.5,
    color = "#212427",
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  colorspace::scale_fill_continuous_diverging(
    palette = "Blue-Red 3",
    mid = 0.50,
    alpha = 0.5,
    limits = c(0, 1),
    name = "Transition \nProbability"
  ) +
  labs(x = "To", y = "From") +
  facet_wrap(~transition, labeller = labeller(transition = c(
    "obs" = "Observed Transitions", "pred" = "Predicted Transitions"
  ))) +
  theme_pres() +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(size = rel(0.8), face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "none")
```

## Simulation Study

### Simulation design

::: incremental
- Simulated $N = 10{,}000$ individuals across $t = 3$ waves.
- For each subject $i$, time-invariant and initial time-varying covariates $(x_1 \dots x_5)$ were generated to [mimic empirical datasets]{.alert}.
- $y_{it}$ is a categorical state for individual $i$ at wave $t$, with three possible states $(1, 2, 3)$.
- Additionally, $y_{it}$ followed [3 different scenarios]{.alert}.
:::

## Simulation Study

### Simulation design

- [Base models]{.alert} $\rightarrow$ treats all observations independently.
    - $y \sim x_1 +x_2 + x_3$
- [Additive models]{.alert} $\rightarrow$ includes previous state additively.
    - $y \sim x_1 +x_2 + x_3 + y_{t-1}$
- [Multiplicative models]{.alert} $\rightarrow$ includes previous state multiplicatively.
    - $y \sim (x_1 +x_2 + x_3) \times t_{t-1}$

### Simulation design

## Simulation Study {footer=false}

### Simulation design

From each fitted model we compute an individual-specific predicted transition matrix:

<br>

::: fragment
\begin{equation}
\hat{P} =
\begin{bmatrix}
P(y_t=1 | y_{t-1}=1) & P(y_t=2 | y_{t-1}=1) & P(y_t=3 | y_{t-1}=1) \\
P(y_t=1 | y_{t-1}=2) & P(y_t=2 | y_{t-1}=2) & P(y_t=3 | y_{t-1}=2) \\
P(y_t=1 | y_{t-1}=3) & P(y_t=2 | y_{t-1}=3) & P(y_t=3 | y_{t-1}=3) \\
\end{bmatrix}
\end{equation}
:::

<br>

:::: fragment
::: {.callout-important icon="false" collapse="true"}
## We then compare $P$ and $\hat{P}$ via several **distance metrics**.
:::
::::

## Simulation Study {footer=false}

### Distance metrics

- **Frobenius Norm**
  $\rightarrow ||\mathbf{D}||_F = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n} d_{j,k}^2}$

- **Manhattan Distance**
  $\rightarrow ||\mathbf{d}||_1 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} |d_i|$

- **Maximum Absolute Error**
  $\rightarrow \max(|d_i|)$

- **Mean Absolute Error**
  $\rightarrow \frac{1}{n} ||\mathbf{d}||$

- **Root Mean Squared Error**
  $\rightarrow \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} ||\mathbf{D}||_F$

- **Correlation Dissimilarity**
  $\rightarrow 1 - \rho(\text{vec}(\mathbf{P}), \text{vec}(\mathbf{\hat{P}}))$

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## We also compare against AIC and BIC
:::

## Simulation Study {footer=false}

### Results

![](files/images/results.png){height=5in}

## Goodness of fit diagnostics for Markov Models

### Conclusions

- For small sample sizes both [Manhatten Distance]{.alert} and [Mean Absolute Error]{.alert} perform equiviently, and sometimes better than standard measures as assertaining the true model.
- For large sample sizes AIC and BIC assertain the true model almost all the time.

<br>

:::: fragment
::: {.callout-tip icon="false" collapse="true"}
## We have developed goodness of fit metrics for small sample sizes
:::
::::
